title: Wanted: Senator-heroes
primary_topics: Senate gridlock as a 'political purgatory' befuddling a people already reeling from high prices, criminality, flood control corruption, the VP impeachment trial and an earthquake -- salvation should come from a senator casting the decisive 13th vote, not from the Supreme Court

Gatchalian group's view -- the 12 senators present on June 3 were a valid quorum, per Avelino v. Cuenco (1949): only senators physically present count; the 1987 quorum provision (Art. VI, Sec. 16[2]) is the same as the 1935 text

Cayetano bloc's view -- electing the Senate President or any other officer needs an absolute majority of 13 of 24, including detained or fugitive members, per Art. VI, Sec. 16[1]; both blocs agree 13 is needed for the Senate President

The real controversy -- the vote needed for a quorum and for 'other' officers such as the President Pro Tempore; CJP's ponencia in Defensor-Santiago v. Guingona (1998): Constitution 'dead silent' on other officers, left to Senate rules (Rule II, Sec. 2) -- the Senate is the sole judge of its own choices
Judicial restraint -- despite the Court's expanded power to check grave abuse of discretion, it should not be dragged into partisan landmines until internal political remedies are exhausted

Saint Paul analogy -- the flawed persecutor blinded on the road to Damascus and redeemed; the elusive 13th senator can break the deadlock and be remembered as an institutional hero, wiping away past transgressions

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban says the Senate gridlock has plunged the nation into a political purgatory, befuddling a people already reeling from high prices, rising criminality, flood control corruption, the Vice President's impeachment trial and a recent earthquake. Amid a clamor for the Supreme Court to step in, he argues that the Senate's salvation should come from a senator (or senators) willing to attend sessions and cast the decisive 13th vote without judicial intervention. To be fair, he sets out both views. The Gatchalian group, led by newly elected Senate President Pro Tempore Sherwin Gatchalian, holds that the 12 senators who stayed in session on June 3 were a valid quorum, citing Avelino v. Cuenco (1949), which counted only senators physically present, and noting that the 1987 quorum provision is the same as the 1935 text. The Cayetano bloc, led by previously elected Senate President Alan Peter Cayetano, contends that electing the Senate President or any other officer needs 13 of 24 votes, including those detained or hiding as fugitives, under Article VI, Section 16(1); both sides agree that 13 is needed for the Senate President. The real controversy is the vote needed for a quorum and for other officers such as the President Pro Tempore. In Defensor-Santiago v. Guingona (1998), which CJP wrote, the Court observed that the Constitution is 'dead silent' on selecting other officers and leaves it to the Senate's rules, so the Senate is the sole judge of its own choices. The solution therefore rests on the heroism of even one patriotic senator; the Court should not be dragged into partisan landmines until internal remedies are exhausted. Recalling Saint Paul, the persecutor redeemed on the road to Damascus, CJP says the senator who breaks the deadlock would be remembered as an institutional hero. History never forgets the sinners, but more so those who find the courage to redeem themselves.
